ideas.title: The people who actually own the bond market are not selling. They are buying more.
ideas.dek: Pensions, insurers and funds now hold a net position worth 46% of the entire 10-year Treasury futures market — the 99th percentile of sixteen years of records, with the four largest readings ever all set since mid-July. Betting against this crowd has been the losing side of the trade.
ideas.call: Over the next six to twelve months the 10-year Treasury yield is more likely to fall than rise. The market's largest holders are near a record share of it, past extremes this deep were followed by lower yields in most cases, and a 10-year note pays 4.69% while you wait.

the_trade.buy: 10-year US Treasury notes — the bonds themselves, or a plain 10-year Treasury fund
the_trade.sizing: A core holding, not a trading position. The measured edge is roughly two tenths of a point of yield over six months — about 1.5% of price on a 10-year note — on top of the 4.69% the note pays for holding it. The case is collect-the-yield-with-a-tailwind, not a bet on a crash.

ideas.instrument: 10-year US Treasury notes, held outright, six to twelve months

edge.summary: Weekly CFTC data splits futures ownership by who holds it. Asset managers — pensions, insurers, mutual funds — now hold a net long worth 46% of all 10-year futures outstanding, the 99th percentile of sixteen years. The reflex reading of a record position is that it must unwind. Measured, the opposite held: after extremes this deep, yields fell over the following six to twelve months.

backtest.window: Weekly CFTC Traders in Financial Futures reports, January 2010 to August 2026 — 868 reports, the 10-year contract's pre- and post-2022 listings joined. Entry when asset managers' net position, as a share of open interest, ranks at or above the 95th percentile of its own history to that date (a trailing calculation, so no reading uses information that did not yet exist). Episodes at least nine weeks apart.
backtest.result: Across the 19 episodes with six months of history, the 10-year yield fell a median 0.18 points and rose in only 37% of cases. Across the 16 with twelve months, it fell a median 0.11 points and rose in only 25% of cases.
backtest.baseline: Over the same sixteen years, the yield's median six-month change was +0.03 points, rising 51% of the time; the median twelve-month change was +0.19 points, rising 57% of the time.

ideas.variant: Consensus is on the record and it is the other side of this trade: Bloomberg's Markets Pulse survey published August 19 carried the headline that the US 10-year yield will top 5% this year, and the argument everywhere is supply — deficits force yields up regardless of buyers. The positioning data says the reversal traders fear would have to be sold by pensions and insurers, who buy bonds to meet obligations decades out and have historically kept accumulating through their own extremes, while the investors actually positioned for higher yields — hedge funds, net short 40% of the market — are the ones who have to buy if they are wrong.
thesis: Start with who owns it. Asset managers hold a net long worth 46.2% of all open 10-year Treasury futures, the 99.1st percentile of 868 weekly reports back to January 2010 — and the four largest readings in the entire series were all set between July 14 and August 4 of this year. This is not a stale extreme; it is still being built.

What followed past extremes runs against the reflex. In the 19 completed episodes since 2010 where this share crossed the 95th percentile of its own history, the 10-year yield fell a median 0.18 points over the next six months and rose in only 37% of them — against a coin-flip baseline. At twelve months the yield rose in only a quarter of the episodes.

The holder matters. Pensions and insurers buy bonds to meet obligations decades away; they are structurally slow to reverse. The same fade-the-extreme instinct that is correct for fast money has been wrong for this cohort — their extremes have marked the middle of moves in yield, not the end.

You are paid more to hold the long bond than at any point in a decade. The term premium — the extra yield for holding a 10-year note instead of rolling short-term bills — is 84 basis points, the 99.7th percentile of the last ten years, and the after-inflation yield of 2.35% is at the 98th percentile of the same window. The valuation argument and the positioning argument point the same way.

The fast money is on the other side, in size. Hedge funds are net short 39.8% of open interest — the 5th percentile of the sixteen-year record. A standoff this wide between record real-money length and deep fast-money shorts has an asymmetry: if yields fall, the shorts must buy into a market whose biggest owners are not selling.

levels.trigger: Asset managers' share of the 10-year futures market crossed the 95th-percentile entry level in mid-2025 and stands at the 99.1st percentile as of the August 18 report, with the 10-year at 4.69% and the term premium at a ten-year high.
levels.invalidation: A weekly close in the 10-year yield at or above 5.00% — a level it has not closed at since 2007 in our data (the October 2023 peak was 4.98%). Through there, the market is repricing government debt itself, and the positioning case is overruled.
levels.target: 10-year yield at or below 4.50% within six months — the median historical move from these extremes — with the note's running yield collected along the way.

sections.title: Setting the stage
sections.prose: Every week the CFTC publishes who holds Treasury futures, split into types: asset managers (pensions, insurers, mutual funds — the slow, deep-pocketed money), leveraged funds (hedge funds — the fast money), and dealers. Most positioning commentary lumps these together. Separated, they tell a story the combined number hides: the slow money's net position has grown to 46% of the whole 10-year market, the largest concentration in sixteen years of records, while the fast money is short 40% — near its own record the other way. This note is about which of those two crowds history says to stand with.

sections.title: Why not just fade the record long?
sections.prose: Because it has been tried, in this exact market, and it lost. The instinct that a full position must unwind works for fast money, whose positions are bets. It has failed against asset managers, whose positions are obligations: a pension buying 10-year notes to fund benefits in 2045 does not sell because its futures share hit a percentile. In the nineteen completed episodes since 2010 where their share crossed the 95th percentile of its own history, yields fell over the following six months in nearly two thirds of them — and over twelve months, in three quarters. The record long has been the signal, not the warning.

sections.title: What the other side says
sections.prose: The case for 5% yields — Bloomberg's survey headline of August 19 — rests on supply: deficits mean more bonds than buyers, whoever the buyers are. It is a serious argument and 2026 has been its year; the failing recent episodes in our own backtest are what that argument looks like in the data. Two things answer it here. The term premium at a ten-year high means the market has already repriced a great deal of that supply risk into today's yield — that is precisely what a term premium is. And the Treasury's own buyback operations, the first of which lands September 9, put a price-insensitive buyer on the other side of the supply story for the first time in this cycle.

sections.title: Dates that decide it
bullets: 2026-09-04 — Jobs report. Another negative payroll month makes the case; a strong one hurts it.
2026-09-09 — The Treasury's first bond buyback operation of the programme announced this month.
2026-09-11 — Consumer prices (CPI). The number most able to reprice the whole curve.
2026-09-16 — Fed decision. A cut with soft labour data behind it is the cleanest path to lower long yields.
2026-10-28 — Fed decision, second chance at the same.

ideas.other_side: The honest case against is that 2026 has been the year this signal broke. The three most recent completed episodes — September 2025, November 2025, February 2026 — all failed, with the yield rising up to half a point over the following six months, the longest failing streak in the sample, and the April entry is under water too. If deficits and Treasury supply now set the price of the long bond, then record real-money ownership just means the owners are wrong at growing scale, and the term premium at a ten-year high is not compensation on offer but a warning of more to come. Two structural caveats belong here as well: the contract changed listing in 2022 and asset managers' share has climbed structurally since the Fed stepped back from the market, so part of today's percentile reflects a regime change rather than conviction; and the signal only separates from the baseline at the 95th percentile and above — at the 85th to 93rd it shows nothing — so the edge lives in a thin tail of 22 episodes.
risks: A hot CPI print on September 11 or a Fed that does not cut on September 16 repricing the front end and dragging the 10-year with it.
Supply: quarterly refunding announcements keep growing, and a deficit-driven selloff ignores positioning entirely — that is exactly what the three recent failed episodes looked like.
The edge is a thin tail: 22 episodes in sixteen years, and only the deepest extremes carry it. Below the 95th percentile the signal shows nothing at all.

The 2022 contract relisting and the Fed's exit from the market shifted the level of asset managers' share structurally upward; the percentile overstates how unusual today is by some unknowable amount.
ideas.so_what: A 10-year Treasury bought today pays 4.69% a year while the market's deepest-pocketed owners keep adding to a record position — and past extremes like this one were followed by lower yields, not the unwind the street is calling for. Buy the note or a plain 10-year Treasury fund, and get out if the yield closes a week at 5% or higher.

scorecard.note: Scored as the price return of a 10-year par bond from the yield series, against the alternative the term-premium argument competes with: staying in short-dated Treasuries.

reconciles.prose: The August 16 note sells ordinary 10-year Treasuries, dollar for dollar, to buy their inflation-protected twins — and this note buys the ordinary ones back. That is not the contradiction it looks like, because the two notes answer different questions. The August 16 trade is a swap: it wins if inflation compensation is repriced upward, and it does not care whether yields rise or fall. This note is about the level: it wins if yields fall. A reader who takes both ends up simply owning 10-year TIPS — the sold Treasuries in the first trade and the bought Treasuries in this one cancel out. Read together, the house view is one sentence: own the 10-year Treasury market, and prefer the inflation-protected version of it while inflation insurance is priced this cheaply. A reader taking only one idea should take this one; it is the simpler position.

ideas.title: The volatility curve is at its steepest in five years. That has been a pay cut, not a warning.
ideas.dek: The S&P's 30-day implied volatility is trading at 0.77 times its three-month — the flattest near-date reading in five years of daily data. In the 37 independent episodes since 2011 that reached this percentile, the index returned +4.36% over the following six months against a +6.63% unconditional baseline, and +10.20% over twelve against +13.48%. The drawdown odds barely moved. What changed was the pay, not the risk — and the sleeve that gained relative ground in those windows was banks, which today sit mid-range while the Nasdaq's lead over the S&P sits at the 94th percentile.
ideas.instrument: US bank equities against the S&P 500
ideas.call: US bank shares are positioned to out-return the S&P 500 over the next six months, and the index itself to pay materially less than its normal return for the same downside risk, because the 30-day-to-three-month volatility curve is at its steepest contango in five years.

the_trade.buy: US bank equities — the KBW-style bank complex, held outright.
the_trade.funded_by: Trimming the most concentrated part of existing US index exposure: the Nasdaq-100-weighted leadership, whose relative-strength ratio against the S&P sits at the 94th percentile of five years and whose own implied volatility is 45% above the S&P's, the 96th percentile of that relationship.
the_trade.expression: An allocation shift inside equity exposure. Nothing is sold short, nothing is borrowed, and total equity weight does not change. The claim is about which equities pay, not about whether to own them.
the_trade.size: A tilt, not a reversal — the base rate is a 60% hit rate on the relative leg, which supports moving a slice, not the book.
the_trade.hedge_note: If protection is wanted alongside this, it is unusually cheap here in absolute terms: three-month S&P implied volatility sits at 18.46, the 28th percentile of five years. The steep curve is precisely what makes the far date inexpensive.

edge.summary: The slope of the S&P volatility curve — 30-day implied divided by three-month implied — has been a usable conditioning variable for the next two to four quarters of equity return, in a direction most readers guess wrong. Steep contango is read as complacency and therefore as danger; the measured outcome is not danger but dilution. Returns compress toward half the unconditional rate while the frequency and depth of drawdowns stay where they were. The relative result is the more actionable half: banks, a sleeve nobody associates with the options market, gained ground against the index in these windows at a 60% rate against a 44% baseline.

backtest.window: 2011-12 to 2026-08 (daily, 5,049 sessions of VIX/VIX3M from 2006-07; ranked on a causal trailing five-year percentile so no observation uses data it could not have had)
backtest.result: Entering at a curve reading in the bottom 5th percentile: S&P +0.40% at one month, +2.19% at three, +4.36% at six, +10.20% at twelve. Six-month hit rate 74%. Banks against the S&P: +1.72% at six months (median +3.69%), hit rate 60%. Nasdaq's excess over the S&P falls to +0.96 percentage points at six months. Probability of a 10% drawdown inside six months: 22%.
backtest.baseline: Unconditional over the identical span, sampled every fifth session: S&P +1.11% / +3.34% / +6.63% / +13.48% at one, three, six and twelve months, six-month hit rate 82%. Banks against the S&P: -1.11% at six months (median -1.42%), hit rate 44%. Nasdaq's excess over the S&P +2.03 percentage points. Probability of a 10% drawdown inside six months: 19%.
backtest.robustness: The direction holds in all three sub-periods (2011-2015 -2.03pp, 2016-2020 -1.28pp, 2021-2026 -4.33pp) and at every threshold tested from the 2nd to the 20th percentile (-1.28pp to -2.40pp). Episodes are separated by at least 42 trading days, so overlapping weeks are not counted as independent observations.

ideas.variant: Consensus reads a 14 handle on the VIX and a curve this steep as complacency, and complacency as a setup for a fall — the standard risk-manager reflex is to cut equity exposure and buy protection into it. The measured record disagrees with the second half of that. Drawdown frequency after these readings is statistically indistinguishable from any other day; what actually degrades is the return you are paid for carrying unchanged risk. That is a different problem with a different answer: not less equity, but different equity. Almost nobody runs the sector question off the volatility surface, because the two live on different desks.
thesis: The signal is a slope, not a level. A VIX of 14.25 on its own is unremarkable — the 15th percentile of five years, and low volatility has been the market's resting state for most of the last decade. What is rare is 14.25 sitting against a three-month reading of 18.46. That ratio, 0.77, is the 0.6th percentile of the last five years: the options market has priced the coming month as calmer relative to the coming quarter than on all but a handful of days since 2021. The market is not saying nothing will go wrong. It is saying nothing will go wrong soon.

What follows is dilution, not danger, and the distinction is the whole note. Across 37 independent episodes since December 2011, the six-month return after a reading this steep was +4.36% against +6.63% unconditionally, and the twelve-month was +10.20% against +13.48% — roughly a third of the return removed. Meanwhile the probability of at least a 10% peak-to-trough drawdown inside six months was 22% conditionally against 19% unconditionally, and at three months the conditional figure was actually the lower of the two, 8% against 11%. You are not being handed more risk. You are being handed less compensation for the risk you already have, which is a portfolio-construction problem rather than a hedging one.

Banks are the sleeve the record points to, and they are not extended. In those same 37 windows the bank complex gained on the S&P at a 60% rate with a median relative gain of 3.69%, against a 44% rate and a median loss of 1.42% for a randomly chosen entry — a spread that widens rather than decays as the horizon extends, reaching +4.56 percentage points at twelve months. The setup matters as much as the statistic: the bank-to-index ratio today sits at the 44.6th percentile of five years, squarely mid-range, so this is a rotation into something ordinary rather than a chase of something already run.

The funding leg is where the concentration sits, and the options market is quietly agreeing. Nasdaq-100 implied volatility is 20.72 against the S&P's 14.25, a ratio of 1.45 that ranks in the 96th percentile of five years — the options market is charging near-record relative premium to insure the index whose relative-strength ratio against the S&P is simultaneously at its 94th percentile. In the backtested episodes, the Nasdaq's structural excess return over the S&P more than halved, from +2.03 percentage points to +0.96 at six months. The premium for concentration has historically been at its thinnest exactly when it was priced at its dearest.

The cross-asset reading is the tell that this is about equities specifically and not a general calm. Gold implied volatility sits at 1.68 times the VIX, the 97th percentile of the relationship since 2008; crude oil implied volatility at 3.48 times, the 94th percentile since 2007. Rate volatility is at the 14th percentile of five years. So the hedging bid has not disappeared from the system — it has migrated into metal and energy and out of the equity index. When one asset's insurance is being marked down while every other asset's is being marked up, the interesting question is what the equity market thinks it knows.

levels.trigger: Already live. The curve closed at 0.7719 on 14 August, its third consecutive session inside the bottom 5th percentile of five years, which is the entry condition the 37 backtested episodes were defined on.
levels.invalidation: The VIX ÷ VIX3M ratio closing above 1.00 — outright backwardation. That is not a worse version of this setup, it is the opposite one: in the same dataset, readings in the top 5th percentile preceded six-month S&P returns of +8.97% against a +6.63% baseline. If the curve inverts, this note's premise has been replaced rather than damaged, and the allocation shift should be unwound. Separately, if the bank-to-S&P ratio runs through the 75th percentile of five years before the six months are out, the relative leg has done its work early.
levels.target: The relative leg: banks gaining roughly 3 to 4 percentage points on the S&P over six months, the conditional median of the backtested episodes. The absolute expectation for the index over the same window is a positive but below-par +4.4%, and the note is not built on the index falling.

ideas.other_side: The honest counter is that 74% of these episodes still made money over six months, and the twelve-month hit rate was 85% — statistically identical to the 86% unconditional. Acting on a return-degradation signal as though it were a direction signal is the most likely way to lose money on this note, because the modal outcome remains a rising market. There is also a live mechanism argument for staying put: steep contango is itself the product of persistent volatility-selling flows, and those flows are supportive of equity prices for as long as they persist, which can be quarters. And the bank leg is the weaker of the two claims — a 60% hit rate against a 44% baseline over 37 observations is a real edge but a thin one, and the effect is concentrated at the tightest thresholds where the sample is smallest.
risks: Sample size. Thirty-seven independent episodes over roughly fifteen years is enough to reject coincidence but not enough to be precise about magnitude. The 2021-2026 sub-period, where the effect is largest at -4.33 percentage points, contains only eight of them.

The relative leg is thinner than the absolute one. Banks beat the index in 60% of episodes; that is 22 of 37, and a handful of different outcomes would move it materially. The median relative gain of +3.69% is more reliable than the mean of +1.72%, which tells you the distribution has a left tail.

Bank-specific risk is not volatility-structure risk. A credit event, a regional funding scare, or a sharp curve flattening would overwhelm this signal entirely. The high-yield-to-investment-grade spread at 271 basis points is near the tight end of its post-2011 range, which is a comfort today and a vulnerability if it moves.

The signal conditions returns; it does not time them. The one-month conditional return of +0.40% against +1.11% is a small difference on a noisy series, and nothing in this work identifies when inside the six months the underperformance arrives.

Regime dependence. Every episode in this sample sits inside a long equity bull market with two short interruptions. A dataset that began in 1998 rather than 2011 might read differently, and VIX3M does not exist before 2006 to check.
ideas.so_what: This is a note about what you are being paid, not about what is about to happen. The equity market is offering roughly two-thirds of its usual six-month return for an unchanged amount of downside — and it is offering the thinnest version of that inside the most concentrated part of the index, at the moment the options market is charging the most to insure it. The response is a tilt within equities toward a sleeve that is neither expensive nor extended, not a reduction in equities. If the volatility curve inverts, the setup reverses and so should the tilt.

ideas.title: Two prices for the same insurance, and only one of them is cheap
ideas.dek: The inflation compensation inside a 10-year Treasury is 2.27% — the 31st percentile of three years. Gold, which insures against the same thing, sits at the 85th percentile of three years and the 98th of its history since 2000. In the eighteen episodes since 2006 when those two hedges have been priced this far apart, the bond market's number was the higher one six months later in three cases out of four. Unconditionally it is a coin flip.
ideas.call: Over the next two to three quarters the inflation compensation inside a 10-year Treasury — 2.27%, the 31st percentile of three years — is likelier to widen than to narrow. Gold prices the same risk at the 85th percentile of three years, and when the two have disagreed this far, the bond market's number is the one that has moved.

the_trade.buy: 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS). The principal is adjusted upward with the consumer price index, so the holder is repaid in money that keeps its purchasing power.
the_trade.sell: Ordinary 10-year Treasury notes of the same maturity, dollar for dollar. Same issuer, same maturity date, same credit — the only thing that changes is whether the payout is fixed or indexed to inflation.
the_trade.sizing: Matched maturity and matched money. Nothing is sold short and no borrowing is involved: this is a swap of one Treasury for another. The position pays off if inflation over the life of the bond runs above 2.27% a year, or if the market simply revises its guess upward; the profit and loss is the difference between two Treasuries, not a view on whether yields rise or fall.

edge.summary: Two markets that price protection against the same risk are far apart. The 10-year inflation breakeven sits in the bottom third of its trailing three-year range while gold sits in the top fifteen percent of its own, and industrial commodity prices are at the top of their range with copper in the 99th percentile of three years. The gap between the two hedges — not the low breakeven on its own — is what the measurement is built on.

backtest.window: Daily, 29 December 2006 to 14 August 2026 — 4,900 observations, being every day on which a trailing three-year percentile exists for both gold and the 10-year inflation breakeven. Condition: gold in the top 15% of its own trailing three years AND the breakeven in the bottom 35% of its own. That fires on 1,079 days, which collapse to 18 distinct episodes.
backtest.result: At six months the breakeven was wider a median of 9.5 basis points counting one observation per episode, with 75% of the 16 completed episodes positive; across 18 non-overlapping six-month windows the median was +12 basis points with 72% positive. At three months the two counting methods disagree — +15 basis points across 31 non-overlapping windows (71% positive) but only +3.5 basis points on the stricter one-per-episode count (56%) — which is why the horizon on this note is set at six months rather than three.
backtest.baseline: Unconditional over the same sample: the six-month change in the breakeven has a median of +1.5 basis points with 52% of 40 non-overlapping windows positive, and the three-month change a median of −1 basis point with 48% of 81 windows positive. The control that matters more: on the days when the breakeven is equally low but gold is NOT in the top 15% of its range, the six-month median is +3.0 basis points with 57% positive — roughly a third of the conditional result. The low breakeven alone is worth something; the disagreement between the two hedges is worth most of it.

ideas.variant: Consensus holds these as two separate conversations. The breakeven is read as the bond market's inflation forecast — a serious, liquid, professional number. Gold is read as a story about central bank buying, government debt and geopolitics, and therefore as saying nothing about the consumer price index at all. Both instruments are nevertheless bought by people who want to be protected from the same outcome, and they are currently priced as if that outcome has very different odds. The variant view is not that gold is right and the bond market is wrong; it is that a 54-percentile gap between two prices for one risk has historically closed from the cheaper side, and the cheaper side is the one you can buy from the US Treasury.
ideas.instrument: 10-year inflation breakeven — TIPS held against nominal 10-year Treasuries, two to three quarters
ideas.horizon: Two to three quarters. The measured edge holds under both counting methods at six months and only one of them at three, so this is a six-month proposition with an entry window, not a multi-year holding.
thesis: The 10-year Treasury yields 4.68%, the 96th percentile of three years — but almost none of that is about inflation. The real yield is 2.41%, the 97th percentile of three years and the 99th of ten. The inflation compensation left over is 2.27%, the 31st percentile of three years. The bond market is charging a great deal to lend money and almost nothing to insure the lender against prices.

Every other market that prices the same risk disagrees. Gold at $4,363.60 is in the 85th percentile of its trailing three years and the 98th of its history back to August 2000. Copper at $6.5925 a pound is in the 99th percentile of three years and sits 1.7% under the highest price in that series, set on 5 August 2026. Wheat is in the 96th percentile of three years. None of that is the behaviour of a world in which inflation compensation belongs in the bottom third of its range.

The measurement supports the divergence rather than the level. Conditioning only on a low breakeven gives a six-month median of +8 basis points; adding the requirement that gold be expensive at the same time raises it to +12, and the mirror case — low breakeven, gold not expensive — gives +3. The gap between two hedges carries the information, which is why this is not simply a bet that a cheap thing gets less cheap.

The position is deliberately neutral on the direction of interest rates. In the historical episodes the widening came mostly from the nominal yield moving up — a median +18 basis points at three months against +6 for the real yield — so a reader who owns this expressed as TIPS against nominal Treasuries collects the gap whether yields rise or fall. That matters right now, because there is no confident view available on the level of rates into a September FOMC meeting that follows a jobs report showing payrolls at −23,000.

The most extended position in our own positioning data sits on the other side of the leg being sold. Asset managers — pension funds, insurers, real-money accounts — hold a net long in 10-year Treasury futures equal to 46.8% of open interest, the 97.5th percentile of the 236 weekly reports since February 2022. Real money is maximally long the nominal bond. Nobody is that long the indexed one.

levels.trigger: A 10-year breakeven at or below 2.30%. It is 2.27% as of 14 August, so the entry is live; scale in ahead of the 11 September consumer price report rather than after it.
levels.invalidation: A weekly close in the 10-year breakeven below 2.10% — the bottom decile of the past three years — or a payrolls print below −100,000 on 4 September or 2 October. Either says the market is pricing a demand shock rather than an inflation one, and this position loses on both legs in that world.
levels.target: A 10-year breakeven of 2.39%, which is the +12 basis point six-month median the base rate implies from 2.27% and sits inside the 2.02%–2.50% range of the past three years. There is no case here for a return to the 3.02% of April 2022.

sections.title: What you are actually buying
sections.prose: A nominal Treasury pays a fixed number of dollars. A Treasury Inflation-Protected Security pays a smaller fixed rate on a principal that grows with the consumer price index. The difference between the two yields — 2.27% today at ten years — is the annual inflation rate at which the two end up in the same place. Buy the indexed bond and sell the ordinary one and you own nothing except that number: same issuer, same maturity, no credit risk taken, no money borrowed. If inflation over the coming years averages more than 2.27%, or if the market's estimate of it moves up before then, the indexed bond wins. If prices run cooler than that, the ordinary one does.

sections.title: Setting the stage — which product this is
sections.prose: Match the horizon to the signal. This one is a measurement about a gap between two prices, and gaps between prices close over months, not over years. The evidence is clean at six months under both ways of counting it and ambiguous at three. So the honest description is a two-to-three-quarter position with a defined level that proves it wrong, entered while the breakeven sits below 2.30%. It is not an inflation forecast, it is not a call on the level of yields, and it is not a view a reader should still be holding in 2028.

sections.title: Why the counting method matters
bullets: The condition fires on 1,079 separate days since 2006. Treated as 1,079 independent observations it would look overwhelming, and it would be wrong — those days sit inside 18 episodes, and days within an episode tell you the same thing repeatedly.
Two stricter counts are reported instead. Non-overlapping windows: take one observation, skip forward the full horizon, take the next. One-per-episode: take only the day the condition first fires.
At six months both agree — +12 basis points and 72% positive on non-overlapping windows, +9.5 and 75% on episode entries, against an unconditional +1.5 and 52%.
At three months they disagree, +15 basis points against +3.5. Where two defensible counts of the same data disagree, the weaker one is the finding. The horizon is set at six months for that reason.

sections.title: Dates that decide it
bullets: 26 August 2026 — personal income and the PCE price index, the inflation measure the Federal Reserve actually targets.
4 September 2026 — the August jobs report. The July report showed payrolls at −23,000; a second negative print is the fastest route to the invalidation level on this trade.
10 and 11 September 2026 — producer prices, then the consumer price index. The single largest scheduled mover of a breakeven inflation rate.

16 September 2026 — the Federal Reserve decision and the updated projections. A committee that signals tolerance for inflation above target while cutting is the outcome this position is positioned for.
14 October 2026 — the next consumer price index, roughly the mid-point of the horizon.

ideas.other_side: The strongest argument against is that a breakeven is not a pure inflation forecast and never has been. Part of the 2.27% is compensation for the fact that inflation-protected Treasuries trade in a thinner market than ordinary ones — buyers demand a discount for that, and it is not an error waiting to be corrected. It can also sit there for a very long time: between 2014 and 2016 the breakeven stayed in the bottom third of its range for more than two years while nothing closed the gap. Second, the gold leg of the argument is a correlation and not a mechanism. Gold is 18% below its January 2026 peak, and a market that has already given back that much may be telling you the inflation hedge is being sold rather than that it is dear. Third, and most seriously, the sample carries one catastrophic observation: the episode entered on 29 July 2008 was 150 basis points lower three months later. Inflation protection is exactly the asset that is marked down when growth breaks, and with payrolls at −23,000 in July this is not a theoretical risk. The trade is a modest median gain against a small chance of a very large loss, and it should be sized as that and nothing else.
risks: A growth accident. If the September or October jobs report confirms contraction, breakevens fall with the demand outlook and both legs move against the position at once. This is the loss that is large rather than the loss that is likely.

The liquidity discount inside TIPS widens instead of narrowing. In a stressed market, indexed Treasuries are sold before ordinary ones — the mechanism that produced the 2008 observation in the sample.

Time. The 2014-2016 precedent had the breakeven in the bottom third of its range for over two years. A six-month horizon can expire while the argument is still intact, which is a real cost even though it is not a large one.

The gold signal is a statistical relationship measured over 18 episodes, not a causal link. Eighteen is enough to be worth acting on and not enough to be sure of, and a reader should hold it that way.

The measured gain is small in absolute terms. A twelve basis point median widening on a ten-year spread is a modest result on the money committed. This is a high-probability, low-magnitude position, and treating it as anything larger is the mistake available here.
ideas.so_what: The bond market is charging the 97th percentile of three years to lend money and the 31st percentile to insure the lender against inflation, at the same moment copper sits in the 99th percentile of three years and gold in the 85th. Two markets are pricing the same risk 54 percentiles apart. The way to own that disagreement is a swap of one Treasury for another — no leverage, no short, no view on the direction of rates — and the honest expectation is a small gain with good odds over six months, not a windfall.

scorecard.note: Re-cut 2026-08-18. The previous block scored the 10-year breakeven as a level change and reported it in pp, so a 1bp widening printed as “+0.01pp” next to equity returns in per cent — not comparable in unit or in size. The trade is now its two actual sides: long 10y TIPS, short duration-matched 10y nominals, each converted from its own yield to a price return via the modified duration of a par bond at that yield. The net is arithmetically the breakeven move times duration, but it can now be netted, sized and benchmarked. Price return only: the carry on this pair is the realised-versus-breakeven inflation accrual, which we do not observe daily and therefore do not claim.

ideas.title: The most one-sided trade in the market is not on any chart
ideas.call: Over the next one to two quarters the euro is likely to out-return the dollar. Speculators hold the largest dollar long in three years while the dollar's PRICE sits mid-range — the consensus is in the position, not the chart, which is why nothing about the tape looks stretched.
ideas.dek: A dollar long at the 90th percentile of three years with commercial hedgers at the 8th, on a currency trading at the 37th percentile of its own range. Every completed instance of this setup in the sample was followed by a lower dollar three months later — and the sample is small enough that the number of instances matters more than the average.

the_trade.buy: The euro against the dollar (EUR/USD, spot 1.153)
the_trade.short: The dollar — the euro leg is the expression; a short dollar index position is the same trade
the_trade.sizing: Sized to a three-month horizon, not six. The edge measured here decays: the same setup shows a median dollar move of −1.25% at three months and +0.81% at six, so this is not a position to leave on and forget.

edge.summary: Speculative dollar-index positioning at or above the 85th percentile of its three-year distribution, with commercial hedgers at the opposite extreme, and the same trade visible on the crosses — euro shorts at the 10th percentile, sterling at the 8th.

backtest.window: CFTC Commitments of Traders, weekly, 3 August 2023 to 4 August 2026 (156 weeks)
backtest.result: Euro, after speculative positioning at or below the 15th percentile: median +3.18% at three months with 77% of instances positive, and +8.50% at six months with 92% positive (n=26 weeks). Dollar index, after speculative positioning at or above the 85th percentile: median −1.60% at one month with 95% of weeks lower, and −1.25% at three months with 73% lower (n=22 weeks). Those 22 dollar weeks collapse to FOUR independent episodes; three have completed, and all three fell between 4.2% and 6.2% over the following three months.
backtest.baseline: Unconditional over the same 156 weeks: the euro's median three-month return is +0.18% with 52% positive and its six-month is +0.62% with 56% positive; the dollar index's median one-month return is −0.11% with 52% of weeks lower and its three-month is +0.06% with 49% lower. The conditional readings are a genuine departure from a coin flip at one and three months. At SIX months the dollar edge disappears entirely (+0.81% median), which is what sets the horizon on this trade.

ideas.variant: Consensus is not positioned for a weaker dollar and does not think it is taking a consensus position, because the dollar index at 100 is unremarkable — the 37th percentile of its own three-year range, nowhere near an extreme on any chart. The one-sidedness is visible only in the positioning data, at the 90th percentile with commercial hedgers at the 8th. The market is reading price and concluding the trade is not consensus. This note reads the position.
thesis: The position is at an extreme; the price is not. Speculative net length in the dollar index sits at the 90th percentile of the last three years at 43.1% of open interest, and it moved 13 percentile points in the reporting week — new, not a standing condition. The dollar index itself closed at 100.01, the 37th percentile of its three-year range of 96.2 to 110.0. A one-sided position that has not yet been rewarded is a different animal from a one-sided position sitting on a large profit: there is no gain to defend, so the exit is cheaper and faster.

Commercial hedgers are at the opposite extreme on all three legs. Dollar index commercials sit at the 8th percentile, euro commercials at the 90th, sterling commercials on the same side. The positioning feed flags all three as divergences. One market at an extreme is a market view; the same trade expressed three ways with the hedging community taking the other side of each is a consensus.

The base rates favour the fade at this horizon, and stop favouring it after. Euro shorts at or below the 15th percentile have been followed by a median +3.18% three-month euro return against an unconditional +0.18%, and 77% of instances were positive against a 52% coin flip. The dollar side agrees at one and three months and then decays to nothing by six. The trade has a shelf life and the sizing says so.

The same speculators are also at the 87th percentile long gold — and that cannot be right. Both positions have been at or above the 85th percentile in only five of 156 weeks. The daily changes of gold and the dollar index have been NEGATIVELY correlated in 100% of 4,926 rolling one-year windows since 2007, currently −0.33 against a median of −0.39. Speculators are long both sides of a pair that has never once moved together for a year. One of those two books is wrong, and the dollar is the one with the weaker base rate behind it.

sections.title: What the backtest actually says, including where it is thin
sections.prose: Three years of weekly reports is 156 observations, and the dollar signal fires in 22 of them — but those 22 weeks are only FOUR independent episodes, because positioning stays extreme for weeks at a time. Three of the four have completed and all three saw the dollar 4.2% to 6.2% lower three months on. That is a striking run and it is also n=3, which is not a number to size aggressively against. The euro side is better populated at 26 weeks and cleaner against its baseline (+3.18% versus +0.18% at three months; 77% positive versus 52%), which is why the euro is the expression rather than a naked dollar short. Both readings use overlapping weekly windows, which flatters significance; the honest summary is a real effect at one to three months, a small number of genuine episodes behind it, and nothing at all by six months.

sections.title: The idea this note is not making
sections.prose: Speculators are also at the 1st percentile in the Nasdaq 100 and the 2nd in the Russell 2000 — extended shorts in both, with commercials at the 100th percentile on each. That is a more exciting story and it did not survive its own test: after Nasdaq positioning at or below the 10th percentile, the index's median forward return was −0.60% at one month, +2.35% at three and +3.73% at six, against unconditional readings of +2.30%, +6.15% and +11.53%. Buying the extreme was WORSE than buying at random at every horizon. Positioning at an extreme is not a signal by itself; it is a signal in the markets where the base rate says it is one.

sections.title: Dates that decide it
bullets: Every Friday, 3:30 PM — the next Commitments of Traders report. The first thing to watch is whether the dollar percentile falls; the trade works by the position unwinding, so evidence of the unwind is the thesis playing out.
26 August, 8:30 AM — personal income and the PCE price index.
16 September, 2:00 PM — the FOMC decision, with projections. A hawkish dot plot is the single most likely route to the dollar-index-above-103 invalidation.

ideas.other_side: The strongest argument against is the sample. Twenty-two weeks sounds like evidence; four independent episodes, three of them completed, does not. A run of three is exactly the kind of pattern that appears in any three-year window by chance, and the six-month result — a median +0.81% dollar return, no edge at all — is a reminder that whatever is here is short-lived. Second, positioning is a coincident measure and it is reported with a lag: this data is dated 4 August and the unwind may already have begun without the print to show it. Third, a one-sided dollar long can keep being right. If the September projections push the rate differential further in the dollar's favour, commercial hedgers will be on the wrong side and stay there — hedgers are not a smart-money signal, they are the other side of a trade, and treating their extreme as a forecast is the standard way this analysis fails.
risks: n=3 completed episodes. Everything above rests on a run short enough to be luck. Size it as a position with a good base rate, not a high-conviction one.
The signal is reported with a lag. The 4 August data is eight sessions old by publication; a fast unwind would already be in the price and the entry gone.
A hawkish September changes the sign. If the FOMC projections widen the rate gap, the one-sided dollar long becomes the correct dollar long and the invalidation triggers.
The euro is not cheap on price — it sits around the 67th percentile of its own three-year range. This trade is paid by the positioning unwinding, not by the euro being undervalued.
ideas.so_what: The most one-sided position in the market right now is not in equities and is not visible on a price chart — it is a dollar long at the 90th percentile with hedgers on the other side of three separate legs. It has a short shelf life and a thin sample behind it, and it is a far better use of risk over the next two quarters than another observation that stocks are expensive.

scorecard.note: Reviewed 2026-08-18 and deliberately left as ONE leg. The note frames it as “long EUR against a short dollar-index position”, but the dollar is the quote currency of EUR/USD — buying the pair already sells dollars. Adding a short DXY leg would double-count the same exposure, since the euro is roughly 57% of that index. The short-dollar side is inside the instrument. Benchmarked against the dollar index, which is what the consensus position was.
scorecard.funding_inside_instrument: The dollar is the quote currency of EUR/USD, so buying the pair already sells dollars. A separate short dollar-index leg would double the same exposure — the euro is roughly 57% of that index.
